SLOW PACE OF POWER REFORMS 
*642. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI : Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state : 
(a) the reasons for slow pace of reforms in the Power Sector; 
(b) whether this has been one of the main reasons for poor private sector 
response in power generation and transmission; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to accelerate pace of reforms in the 
Power Sector ? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The main reasons which come in the way of rapid progress in power 
sector reforms are: 
(i) High technical losses in distribution specially in rural area. 
(ii) Large scale theft of power in many States. 
(iii) Large scale unmetered supply of electricity and supply through 
faulty meters. 
(iv) Tariff distortions. 
1 

RAJYA  S ABHA [7 May, 2003] 
(v) Inefficient billing and collection,                                                     
(vi) Lack of payment of subsidy by State Governments,                                  
(vii) Lack of investment in transmission and distribution. 
The losses of the State power utilities (without subsidy) in 1992-93 stood at Rs. 4560 
crores and have grown to Rs.33177 crores in 2001-02. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) In the 9th Plan period, against the targeted capacity addition of 17588 
MW through private sector projects, the achievement in the private sector was only 
5061 MW resulting in a shortfall of 71.2%. 
(d) Power sector reforms pose a difficult and complex challenge for the States 
who have exclusive responsibility for distribution which is the core issue in power 
reforms. The Ministry of Power has been encouraging and supporting the States in 
undertaking power sector reforms. Some of the key steps taken in this regard have 
been :— 
(i) Setting up of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and 
encouraging the States to set up State Electricity Regulatory Commissions 
under the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act and State Reform 
Act. 
(ii) The Ministry of Power has signed State-specific Memorandum of 
Understanding/Memorandum of Agreement on power sector reforms 
with 27 States. 
(iii) Under the new Accelerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme, the Central Government is providing financial assistance for 
specific projects in identified distribution circles aimed at bringing about a 
turn around. This has been combined with the provision of incentive by 
way of grant to the States linked to the actual reduction in financial 
losses. 
(IV) Substantial relief has also been given to the State utilities through the 
securitisation of past dues to Central Public Sector Undertakings 
(CPSUs) under the Tripartite Agreement signed with 24 States. 
2 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Stepping up public sector investment in generation through Central 
Public Sector Undertakings and creation of a National Grid to ease 
the power supply situation in States. 
(vi) The Electricity Bill, 2003 which has been passed by both the Houses 
of the Parliament envisages a liberal and competitive framework for 
development of the power sector.

*SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA : Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) details of the new guidelines for roads under PMGSY schemes; 
(b) whether, the Rajya Sabha Members can suggest the road works under 
PMGSY schemes in their given nodal districts, 
 
(c) if so, whether directions have been issued in that connection; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether any recommendation/suggestion of Rajya Sabha Members has 
been ignored in Karnataka; 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
(f) if so, the steps Government propose to take to honour the suggestions 
of Rajya Sabha Members also; and 
(g) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRIANANTHA KUMAR): 
(a) to (g) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The salient features of the revised guidelines issued in January, 2003 are 
enclosed as Statement-I. {See below). 
(b) to (d) As per the revised Guidelines of the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak 
Yojana (PMGSY) issued on 7th January, 2003, the proposals of the Members of 
Parliament are required to be given full consideration. District Panchayats are 
to finalise the list of road works to be taken up under the PMGSY through a 
consultative process involving lower level Panchayati Institutions and elected 
representatives. The list is to be finalised each year in accordance with the 
allocation of funds communicated to the Districts by the State Government. 
The list of Unconnected Habitations (along with the population) in each District 
along with the list of roads identified to connect them as part of the Core 
Network are to be sent to the Members of Parliament, to facilitate them in 
making their suggestions. It will be incumbent upon the District Panchayat to 
ensure that, while framing the proposals, full consideration is given to the 
proposals received from the Members of Parliament, within the framework of 
the Guidelines. 
(e) to (g) One instance has been brought to the notice of the Ministry that road 
works recommended by a Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha) in Karnataka 
have not been included. Government of Karnataka has been addressed in the 
matter. 
Statement-I 
The salient features of the new guidelines for roads under PMGSY schemes 
• Preparation of Rural Roads Plan and Core Network—All roads under 
PMGSY are to be prioritised out of the Core Network keeping in view 
the priorities as per the Guidelines in respect of population size and 
giving preference to new connectivity. 
• Roads specifications—Roads are to be built as per the specifications 
given in Rural Roads Manual published by the Indian Roads Congress 
(IRC: SP20:2002). 
10 

|7 May, 20031 RAJYA SABHA 
• District Level Programmes—The Stale's Allocation will be distributed among 
the Districts giving 80% on the basis of road length required for providing 
connectivity to Unconnected Habitations and 20% on the basis of road length 
requiring Upgradation under the PMGSY. 
• Scrutiny, Approval and Clearance—The proposals prepared by the District 
Panchayats arc to be approved by the State Level Standing Committee. 
Proposals arc to be sent for clearance based on the scrutiny completed by 
Stale Technical Agencies (STAs). 
• Project clearance and Release of funds—Projects will be cleared by Ihc 
Empowered Commillcc of the Ministry of Rural Development and 25% of the 
estimated cost will be released at the time of clearance. Subsequent releases for all 
road works will be subject to utilisation of 60% of earlier released funds as well as 
completion of 80% of the approved road works uplo (but not including) the year 
previous to the current year and other standard conditions 
• Fund management in State—Each State will identify/create a State level 
Autonomous Agency to maintain and operate Bank account to receive project 
funds. This account will be operated by the District Programme 
Implementation Units (DPIUs). 
Execution—No new Agency/ Consultants will be created for execution only. 
• Tendering—The works will be tendered as per Standard Bidding 
Document being circulated to the State Governments by NRRDA. 
Projects will be completed within 6 months except in the case of Hill 
Stales where upto 18 months is allowed. 
Monitoring and Quality Control—Primary responsibility for monitoring will be 
with the District Programme Implementation Unit (DPIU). Each State will 
appoint a State Quality Coordinator and activate the Second-tier Quality 
Control Agency at the State level, independent of the Field Engineers. 
NRRDA will also arrange for sample checks through independent National 
Quality Monitors (NQMs). In case of completed roads being below 'good' 
quality, the contractor must be black-listed. In addition. District Vigilance and 
Monitoring Committee set up by the Ministry of Rural Development will also 
monitor the progress under the Scheme.

Pune and installed alongvvith hardware in all States and Districts Regular 
updating of the software (called OMMS) is an essential requirement for 
continued funding of projects under PMGSY and failure to do so will affect 
releases.

Governments. State Governments have to communicate a satisfactory 
mechanism for the maintenance of rural roads under PMGSY in order to be able 
to receive Programme assistance.

World Bank loan for power reforms in Orissa 
*648. SHRI B. J. PANDA : Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether World Bank has pledged a loan of $ 350 million for power 
reforms in Orissa and whether this loan has now been slashed; if so, how much, 
as reported in the media; 
(b) whether the State Government has approached the Centre for help in 
payment of this loan ; and 
(c) whether this has since been paid in full or in instalments; if so, the 
details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANG ARAM GEETE): (a) 
to (c): A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The World Bank had sanctioned a loan of US $ 350 million for the 
Orissa Power Sector Restructring Project in 1996. The loan was suspended in 
July, 2001 primarily due to persistent delays in release of funds by the State 
Government for the project. It was restored in January, 2002 on the assurance of 
the Government of Orissa that timely release of funds would be ensured. 
From this loan, an amount of US $ 60 million was cancelled in October, 2001 
due to extremely low utilization potential of Orissa. It was proposed to cancel a 
further US $ 50 million for the same reason but on the request of the Government 
of Orissa and after discussion with all stakeholders, it was agreed to cancel only 
US $ 35 million in February, 2003. The loan amount now stands at US $ 255 
million 
An amount of US $ 169.180 million has been disbursed till February, 2003. 
The project is scheduled to end in January, 2004.

that Orissa was the first State to launch a major overhaul of its power sector. The

Statement 
(a) During the year 2002-03, the generation from hydel power stations in 
Kerala was 4865 MUs against the target of 73 98 MUs i.e. less by 34.3%. This

Stations (CGS) in Southern Region (SR) was enhanced from 4% to 
25% during mid-August, 2002 resulting in additional availability of

Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) stations in Eastern Region (ER).

increased from 200 to 300 MW during off-peak period.

commissioned by NTPC in February, 2003 and 14% of generated 
power is being made available to Kerala.

measures to augment availability of power in the State:

Marketing and pricing policies of CIL subsidiaries 
4797. SHRI JANARDHANAPOOJARY: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased 
to state : 
48 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYASABHA 
(a) whether Government has permitted the subsidiaries of Coal India Limited to set 
individual marketing and pricing policies; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that following the notification, one subsidiary is 
encroaching upon the marketing territory of the other; 
(d) if so, the details in this regard, 
(e) whether it is a fact that there is no similarity in the coal production cost of each 
subsidiary, 
(f) if so, whether in the absence of level playing field Government's 
permission is leading to unhealthy competition and liquidation of disadvantaged 
companies; and 
(g) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF COAL (SHRIKARTYA MUNDA): (a) and (b) The 
Government has directed Coal India Limited (CIL) to delegate powers on marketing of coal for 
non-core sector in case of Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL), Western Coalfields Limited 
(WCL) and South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL). Coal pricing is uniform for both 
core and non-core consumers and is decided by CIL for its subsidiaries. 
(c) and ((d) Whereas encroachment upon marketing territory of one subsidiary 
by another is not exactly taking place, a kind of healthy competition between companies 
will certainly develop particularly in non-core sector as consumers will have the 
option to select source of coal best suited to them. 
(e) Yes, Sir. There is no similarity in coal production cost of each subsidiary of CIL. 
The method of mining is different in different subsidiaries. Some subsidiaries mine 
sizeable quantity of coal from underground and some subsidiaries mine more coal 
from open-cast mines, resulting in different cost structure which leads to difference in 
coal production cost of each subsidiary. 
(f) and (g) There is no issue of unhealthy competition and liquidation of 
disadvantaged companies. Coal marketing and pricing policies have been designed 
to subserve the interest of the coal consumers and coal prices have to be competitive to 
offer consumers the best value for their money especially when faced with 
increasing competition from imports. Also, there is no geographical demarcation for 
linkages to or supplies from subsidiaries of CIL. Coal supply from a particular subsidiary 
is primarily dependent on availability of coal, available transport logistics and customer's 
preference based on economic consideration.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (d) A Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) has been 
signed between the Central Government, the Government of Assam and Bodo 
Liberation Tiger (BUT) on 10-2-2003 for a durable solution to the Bodo issues. 
The main terms of the agreement include inter-alia. 
(i) Creation of an Autonomous self-governing body to be known as 
Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) within the State of Assam and 
provision of Constitutional protection under the Sixth Schedule to 
the Constitution of India to the said Autonomous Body. Adequate

Financial powers in respect of subjects entrusted to them. 
(iii) Additional financial assistance of Rs. 100 crore per annum (over and 
above normal plan assistance to State of Assam) for 5 years for projects 
to develop the socio-economic infrastructure in BTC areas. 
(iv) The Government of India agrees to consider favourably the inclusion 
of Bodo language in Devnagri script in the Eighth Schedule of the 
Constitution. 
(v) The Bodo language shall be the official language of BTC subject to 
the condition mat Assamese and English language shall also continue 
to be used for official purposes.

up to impart education in various technologies/vocational disciplines 
such as Information Technology, Bio-technology, Food Processing, 
Rural Industries. Business Management, etc. CIT will be subsequently 
upgraded to a centrally funded State University with technical and 
non-technical disciplines to be run by BTC. 
(vii) The Government of India also agrees to consider sympathetically the 
inclusion of Bodo-Kacharis living in Karbi Anglong and NC Hills 
Autonomous Councils area in the ST (Hill) List of State of Assam.

Reasons  for  floods and  lightening  in  Uttaranchal 
4863. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted any study to ascertain basic 
reasons of severe floods and lightening in Hilly areas of Uttaranchal causing 
great loss to the life and property; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI I. 
D. SWAMI) (a) to (c) The India Meteorological Department has reported that due 
to the following meteorological conditions, Uttaranchal is vulnerable to floods and 
lightning: 
(i)   Passage of monsoon depressions and low pressure areas; 
(ii) Interaction between monsoon depressions/lows with trough in the 
westerlies; and 
(iii) Shifting of the monsoon trough to the foothills of the Himalayas during "Break 
Monsoon" conditions. 
These conditions, along with the fact that the Upper Ganga River Basin lies in 
Uttaranchal State make the area prone to flooding and heavy rainfall due to 
severe thunderstorms, cloud-burst and landslides.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI

4913. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA : Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to refer to the reply to Starred Question No. 417 given in the 
Rajya Sabha on the 18th December, 2002 and state : 
(a) the details of 17 Hydropower projects in the NER on which DPR 
being prepared showing stages of the project preparation, source of funding 
finalized, stages of clearance, target set for commission and executing agency 
entrusted project-wise; and 
(b) the cadre-wise strength of existing staff showing percentage of 
locally recruit and transferred from other establishments of NHPC including 
Headquarter recruitment norms followed and to be followed, the number and 
future of contract labours for regular employment in the Subansiri and 
Dihang Project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA) : (a) At present there are 18 hydro-
electric projects with an aggregate installed capacity of 25890 MW in North-
Eastem Region in the Brahmaputra and Barak Basins for which Detailed 
Project Reports (DPRs) have been prep ared. Out of these, 5 Hydro-electric 
Projects with an aggregate capacity of 359 MW are on going schemes. 
Besides, 4 Hydro-electric schemes have been cleared by Central Electricity 
Authority (CEA) with total capacity as 2890 MW. DPR for one Hydro-
electric schemes of 1500 MW is under examination in CEA after appraisal 
and DPRs for an installed capacity of 21,141 MW have been returned for re-
submission or are under revision with the concerned States/project 
authorities. Details of these schemes with their locations, executing agencies, 
estimated costs, present status etc. are given at Statement I. (see below^ 
(b) As per the information made available by National Hydroelectric 
Power Corporation (NHPC), the cadre-wise strength of existing staff showing 
percentage of locally recruited and transferred from other establishments of 
NHPC including Headquarter, in the Subansiri and Dihang Project (presently 
known as Siang) is given at Statement-II and Statement-Ill. (See below). 
The following norms and procedures are followed for recruitment in 
NHPC : 
Recruitment for the posts of Executives, Supervisors and 
Stenographers are made centrally by giving wide publicity in the press and 
NHPC website. 
Surplus staff from NHPC Head Office as well as from the projects is 
being transferred to these projects from time to time in accordance with the 
requirements. 
If there is any requirement in the workmen cadre, after adjustment of 
surplus staff, the recruitment is done locally through the local employment 
exchanges in accordance with the requirements from time to time. 
Neither Subansiri nor Dihang (Siang) project have any contract labour. 
NHPC has designated an examination centre for effecting centralized 
recruitment on all India basis at Itanagar, Guwahati and Siliguri.

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
Power supply to Maharashtra by Dabhol Power Plant 
4914. DR. AKfflLESH DAS: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Dabhol Power Plant is being revived for augmenting power supply 
to Maharashtra; 
(b) if so, the steps so far taken in this regard; 
(c) the terms of the power purchase agreement, if any signed, revived or 
renewed with Government of Maharashtra and the extent of power supply expected 
from this power plant, indicating the areas to be served thereby; and 
(d) whether Government of Chhattisgarh or other Chhattisgarh Power Plant 
has offered to supply power to Maharashtra and other neighbouring States; if so, 
on what terms? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TOE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI J 
AYAWANTIMEHTA) (a): The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) in regard to the 
Dabhol Power Project was entered into between the Maharashtra State Electricity 
Board (MSEB) and Dabhol Power Company (DPC). Thus, the responsibility to 
restart Phase-I and complete Phase-II of the project lies with the main stakeholders 
viz. MSEB and DPC as well as the Government of Maharashtra. The Indian 
Financial Institutions (IFIs) led by the Industrial Development Bank of India 
(IDBI), having substantial stakes in the Dabhol Power Project, have been trying to 
restructure and revive the Dabhol plant. Government of India has agreed to facilitate 
any amicable solution to the various issues in order to revive/restructure the project. Any 
scheme finalised for revival of the Dabhol project would come as a comprehensive 
package and would have to resolve complex, legal, financial and technical issues. 
While this may take time, as a first step, it has been agreed that an interim revival 
package for restarting Phase-1 be worked out by the concerned agencies. 
(b) It has been decided that the National Thermal Power Corporation 
(NTPC) would act as the Operation & Maintenance Contractor for running Phase-I. 
At the instance of the Government of India (Ministry of Power), a team involving 
representatives from NTPC, M/s. GE India, M/s. Bechtel, IDBI, MSEB and Central 
Electricity Authority carried out a preliminary inspection of the Dabhol power plant 
from October 28 -30,2002 to ascertain its condition and to work out an action plan 
for restart of phase-I. 
148 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) The original PPA in respect of the Dabhol power project provides for 
supply of power by both Phases of the project to the State of Maharashtra. 
Following disputes with DPC, MSEB rescinded the PPA on 23-5-2001 and 
stopped drawing power from the project with effect from 29-5-2003. As a part of 
the ongoing efforts to restart phase-I, Government of Maharashtra has taken a 
decision to allow MSEB to draw power from Phase-I (740MW) of Dabhol 
project at an optimum level of 83% at a tariff of about Rs. 2.80 / KWH on an 
interim basis subject to approval of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory 
Commission (MERC) and High Court of Maharashtra which has appointed a 
receiver for the project, and without prejudice to MSEB / Government of 
Maharashtra's rights and contentions in the pending arbitration/judicial and 
MERC proceedings. Such a tariff level takes into account the current cost of 
naphtha (after remission of all Central & State levies and taxes) with the fuel 
cost being a 'pass through' item. The power supplied by Phase-I of the Dabhol 
project, after it is restarted, will be pooled in to the Maharashtra State Grid for 
supply to the consumers of MSEB. 
For the proposed interim restart, the tariff model is based on the recovery on 
interest on debt at reduced rates (and without any provision for depreciation/ debt

Hydel power potential 
4923. SHRI  SURESH  PACHOURI: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that the country is not able to exploit even 25 per 
cent of its hydel potential; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and

country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA) : (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 17% of the assessed hydro 
potential has been exploited and 6% is under development. Thus, 77% of the 
hydro power potential is yet to be exploited. The constraints which have affected 
hydro development are: 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
—  Constraints of survey and investigation. 
—  Lack of infrastructure. 
—  Geological uncertainties. 
—  Resettlement and rehabilitation issues. 
—  Inter-state aspects. 
—  Environment and forest clearance. 
—  Security problems. 
—  Land acquisition. 
—  Natural calamities like flash floods. 
—  Inadequate funding in some State Sector projects. 
(c) The Government is according high priority to exploit the untapped hydroelectric 
potential in the country. A capacity addition of 14,393 MW from hydro projects is to be 
achieved during the tenth Plan. The hydro-electric projects above 25 MW being 
executed under Central Sector, State Sector and Private Sector are being regularly 
monitored at various levels. Government of India has introduced three-stage 
development of hydro-electric projects in the Central Sector with the object of 
reducing time and cost over-runs during the implementation of these projects A basin 
wise 'Ranking Study' of all the balance hydro-electric potential which is yet to be 
harnessed has been carried out by the CEA and discussions with the State Governments 
have been initiated to finalize an Action Plan for their subsequent development. The first 
lot of 162 projects where pre feasibility reports are to be prepared have recently been 
finalized.

 poverty ratios prepared by the Planning 
 Commission are used for this purpose, while

 of last Census. 
B.   Norms of Releases made to States under poverty alleviation schemes : 
(a) Funds are release under different poverty alleviation schemes to the States 
in two instalments. The second instalment of funds is released only when the 
State/district has utilized 60% of the funds available with it under the 
programme. The first instalment is released automatically without insisting 
on proposal if the implementing Agency has taken the second instalment in 
the previous year without any condition. 
(b) Audit Reports and Utilization Certificates are insisted upon while 
processing the proposals for release of funds. 
181

(c) The cuts are imposed on the funds to be released to the States if 
proposals for second instalment are received late after December. If the 
proposals are received in January, 10% cut on the second instalment is 
effected. If the proposals are received in February, the cut is 20% and if 
the proposals are received in March, the cut is 30%. 
(d) The cany over limit of funds from one year to another is 15% of the 
total allocation during the year.

Four pronged strategy for Rural Development 
4940. SHRIVUAYJ. DARDA: Will theMinisterofRURALDEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state : 
(a) the plans of the Rural Development Ministry to give shape to the Prime Minister's 
statement on adopting four-pronged strategy for rural development-physical and 
electronic connectivity, electricity, market access and electronic services like Telecom 
and Internet; and 
(b) if so, would this planning be an integrated one with time-bound fixed targets, 
adequate budgetary allocation and monitoring to machanism keep an watch on 
progress ? 
THEMMSTEROF STATE INTHEMINISTRY OFRURALDEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ANNAS AHEB M. K. PATIL): (a) Out of four items mentioned, the Ministry of Rural 
Development is concerned, to some extent, with physical connectivity and marketing of 
rural products. 
Government has launched a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme called the Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), which seeks to provide connectivity to all 
unconnected Habitations in the rural areas with a rural population of more than 500 
persons with good all-weather road by the end of the Tenth Five-Year Plan. In respect of 
the Hill States (North-Eastem States including Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and 
Kashmir, Uttaranchal) and Desert Areas, the objective would be to connect Habitations with 
a population of 250 persons and above by 2007. 
Swamjayanti Gram. Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) Guidelines provide for earmarking 
of  20% of the annual allocation as SGSY Programme Infrastructure Fund. This fund could 
be utilized for creation for marketing infrastructure, 
190 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYASABHA 
development of market linkages, processing, packaging etc. Besides, projects 
for development of marketing infrastructure and marketing linkages are being 
sanctioned to the States/DRDAs under SGSY Special Projects. 
As part of marketing initiatives, the Ministry organizes exhibition and sale 
of rural products in SARAS pavilion of the India International Trade fare every 
year. Provision of electricity and electronic services does not come under the 
purview of the Ministry of Rural Development. 
(b) While targets have been fixed only under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak 
Yojana (PMGSY), the budgetary allocation depend on the availability of resorces. 
The Ministry has developed a comprehensive multi-level and multi-tool 
system of monitoring the implementation and impact of the rural development 
schemes, including utilization of funds.

ASANAGOUD A R PATIL): (a) to (c) Government have taken several steps to improve

rationalisation of duty structure in the textile sector and reducing costs 
of machinery critical to technology upgradation;

Deen Dayal Hatkargha Protsahan Yojana 
4950. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA : Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana; 
- (b) if so, the details thereof inter-alia stating the aims thereof, funding pattern, 
incentives and facilities provided under the scheme; 
(c) monitoring mechanism to check the utilization of assistance provided under 
the scheme at the National and State level; 
(d) whether the Government have assessed the impact of the scheme so as to 
decide whether the scheme is to be continued/discontinued keeping in view the huge 
allocation to funds to the scheme; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANGOUDAR.PATIL):(a)Yes,Sir. 
(b) The Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana (DDHPY) aims to provide 
necessary support to upgrade skills and knowledge of weavers along with basic 
inputs for product development and its diversification, strengthen the handloom 
organizations to enable them to provide input to the weavers, ensure availability 
of infrastructure and common facility to develop better products, make weavers 
aware of the demands of the markets and to provide assistance for publicity for 
marketing of handloom goods, improve the mobility of finished handloom 
products from the States of J&K. North Eastern States and Sikkim and also to 
provide suitable marketing incentives to attracts buyers towards handloom 
goods. Funds are provided for margin money, purchase of new looms, jacquards, 
dobbies, accessories, infrastructure support (e.g. setting up of common facility 
centres, water and effluent treatment plant and process houses), publicity, design 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
input, training, marketing incentives, transport subsidy for North Eastern States, Sikkim 
and Jammu & Kashmir and strengthening of handloom organizations. The funding 
pattern between the Centre and the State is in the ratio of 50:50 except in case of 
North Eastern States, Sikkim, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal where the 
sharing is in the ratio of 90:10 (except Marketing Incentives for which the funding 
pattern is 50:50 for all the States). 
(c) As per the scheme, the respective State Governments would be 
responsible for making necessary administrative arrangement for overseeing each 
project and for effective monitoring of its functioning and project. The State 
Governments monitor the projects trough the State Level Project Committee headed by the 
Secretary in-charge of Hondlooms and represented by a member of me Central 
Government. The Government of India also monitors the scheme through its officers and 
the officials of 24 Weavers' Service Centres. 
(d) and (e) The scheme has come into operation only during the year 2000-
2001. It is premature to assess the impact of the scheme as most of the projects are 
at implementation stage only.

Works, and  Improvements to Riding Quality in Kamataka State 
SHRI M. V. RAJASEKHARAN (KARNATAKA): Sir, I would like to draw 
the attention of the Hon'ble Minister for Surface Transport, Government of India, 
regarding an annual plan allocation of Rs. 7500.00 lakhs, which has been made to 
Kamataka State under the National Highway Development Programme original 
works including, improvements of Riding Quality Programme. The total 
expenditure incurred up to the end of December, 2002, was Rs. 5810.68 lakhs as 
against the total allocation of Rs. 7500.00 lakhs. It is assessed that the total grants 
of about Rs. 11,010.68 lakhs is required towards completion of National 
Highway original works, and improvement of Riding Quality Programme works. 
Ten spill over works, sanctioned under IRQP in 2001-02, nineteen fresh works 
sanctioned in 2002-03, and twenty on-going fresh works under IRQP are in 
progress, but are not getting completed due to lack of additional grants. 
So, I urge upon the Central Government to allocate an amount of Rs. 
3510.68 lakhs as additional grants under the National Highway Development 
Programme original works including, IRQP to Kamataka State enabling the State 
Government to complete the works, on a priority basis, since Kamataka has less 
kilometers under the National Highway Development Programme. Thank 
you, Sir. 
Need to Reduce Number of National Holidays 
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ (JAMMU AND KASHMIR): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
am thankful to you forpermitting me to present my Special Mention. 
When the Parliament adjourned recently for ten days due to holidays, I was one 
of many people who thought India had gone too much wrong in allowing a large 
number of holidays to the detriment of national production and productivity. India 
must be the country in the world allowing the greatest number of holidays to 
Government servants, workforce in factories and elsewhere. And, these 
numerous holidays decidedly reduce growth and generate a kind of laziness 
among the people. I would like to remind the August House to consider the 
recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission 
208 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
which had asked for drastic reduction of National Holidays. The Coramision had 
made an earnest recommendation that National Holidays must be reduced to three. 
The Commission, among other things, had recommended, "Apart from the revival 
of six-day week recommended by us, which will result in addition of 52 working days, it 
should suffice if the Central Government offices are closed only on three National 
Holidays—Republic Day, Independence Day and Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. 
Simultaneously, individual employees could be permitted to avail of a large number, say 
about 16, of Restricted Holidays annually to enable the celebration of festivals and other 
occasions of specific significance and interest to them, the list of Restricted Holidays 
being suitably enlarged for this purpose". 
India must take a lesson from the strongest of the monarchies in the world, Saudi 
Arbia, where two-and-half-hour holiday only is allowed on the demise of a monarch 
himself.

Distress sale of paddy by farmers in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Madam, although FCI has opened eight 
purchase centres in Sambalpur and Bargarh disticts to procure paddy directly from 
farmers, it had not purchased a single grain on the pretext of non-availability of 
FAQ paddy thereby facilitating the millers to purchase paddy much below the rate 
fixed by the Government There are allegations from farmers that they have sold their hard-
earned produce much below the Government rate. The FCI should not succumb to the 
pressure of the millers and procure the 
212 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
carry-over stock of rice and also purchase paddy below FAQ with a cut rate, as is being 
done in other States. 
Orrisa has emerged as a surplus State in production of rice but procurement of the 
same is not reaching its targets. The total production in the current agricultural year 
is expected to be 60 lakh MTs and there will be market surplus of 20 lakh MTs during 
this year. 
The State is handicapped, so far as godown space is concerned. There is godown 
capacity of 7.7 lakh MTs out of which 5.8 lakh MTs is used for storage of foodgrains. The 
pace of procurement is badly affected due to lack of storage space which, in turn, hits 
farmers. The FCI should augment storage capacity to the extent of 10 lakh MTs. 
I, therefore, request the Minister of Consumer Affairs to relax specifications in regard 
to procurement of paddy as had been granted to States like Bihar, etc. 
I also request the Central Government to stop distress sale of paddy by farmers 
and make proper arrangements for procurement and storage of paddy in Orissa, 
particularly in Western Orissa.

Delay in Implementation of Projects 
SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Madam, I would like to bring to the notice 
the following facts about the delay in implementation of several projects by several 
Ministries resulting in the escalation of costs. For example, all the Railway proj ects 
worth over Rs. 100 crores are delayed by 13 years resulting in a cost escalation to the tune 
of Rs. 12,000 crores. There are 87 projects with the Railway Ministry which exceeds Rs. 
100 crores, but more than 50 projects are non-starter. Comparing to the other 
Ministries, the Railways are having total allotment of Rs. 23,870 crores. But due to 
inordinate delay in implementation of projects, costs have escalated to the tune of Rs. 
26,352 crores, by the end of last year. As per the latest report, the anticipated cost is Rs. 
35,577 crores. Besides the Railway Ministry, there are other Ministries wherein costs of 
projects have 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
escalated due to delay in implementation. According to the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways, the anticipated cost hike is below Rs. 1000 crores. The Ministry 
of Power, which is having 43 works in hand, has completed only two. The Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas is having 80 proj ects, but managed to complete only 24. 
Totally, there are 366 projects with the Government. Among them, only 34 projects were 
completed by the February end. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme 
Implementation provided these figures. I urge upon the Government to initiate actions 
for timely implementation of the estimated projects in order to avoid escalation in 
costs, especially when our country is already passing through the severe financial 
crisis. 
Request for extension of Kolkata Metro Rail Service up to Netaji Subhash 
Chandra Bose Aiport 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal) : Madam Deputy Chairman, 
Kolkata, the metropolitan city, is having the highest density of population of our 
country. Kolkata has suffered a lot due to partition of Bengal resulting in large-scale influx 
and faced the consequences without any meaningful Central support. The day-time 
population largely differs from the night-time population. Kolkata is having only 6 per 
cent road space and any further addition to the existing hard-pressed surfaced transport 
for widening the limited road, without large-scale demolition and eviction is next to 
impossible. In view of that, construction of new rail routes and extension of the existing 
ones should be made a continuing process over the decades ahead to provide transport 
service to the ever-increasing commuters in Kolkata. 
The existing underground Metro Railways is only having 18 kms. distance from 
Tollygunj up to the Dum Dum Railway Junction. Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Airport is 
located close to the terminal Metro Station at Dum Dum. It would be quite appropriate to 
have the line extended from the Dum Dum Junction up to the Airport, covering only a 
short distance by giving more service to a large number of commuters originating from 
North 24 Parganas, besides, tne users of the Airport. In the capital of Delhi, at the very 
initial stage of planning, connecting the Metro with the Airport, has been correctly 
thought. All over the world, people prefer to travel by the Metro/Tube Railway. I 
request both the Railways and the Urban Development Ministries to consider 
seriously further extension of the Metro Railway up to the Airport, like that of 
Delhi. Thank you.

Pension liabilities on Indian Railways   . 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Kamataka): Thank you, Madam. The 
hon. Railway Minister had presented a please-all Railway Budget for 2003-
04 with the feel-good effect for all and sundry. 
Whatever critical analysis has been made on the floor of both the Houses 
during a debate on the Railway Budget, 2003, it was nothing more than skimming 
the surface and not delving deep into the fiscal malaise, afflicting the railway 
finances. 
The Indian Railways are carrying a pension load that could break its back 
sooner and paralyse the entire economy of the nation. It has already been 
paying its 1.6 million workforce which soaks up 56 per cent of its working expenses. 
This includes pension payments. The Railways have not taken any measures to 
address the problem of increasing pensionary liability on their financial resources. 
Unlike other pension schemes, the Railway pensions were not contributory. Pay 
215 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
outs were charge &, the revenue of the year. They were unfunded. In 1981, an internal 
audit showed that the provision meant for the pension fund was short by Rs. 203 cones. 
Actuaries suggested that the Railways make regular provisions for the pension fund 
liabilities, but the advice was not heeded. If the present trend continues, the Indian 
Railways face the prospect of having to pay out almost half of its gross traffic receipts 
as pensions to its retirees by 2020. 
I urge upon the Central Government to enlighten the House about the present 
quantum of pension liabilities of the Railways and the remedial measures planned Thank 
you

SHRIMATISHAB AN A AZMI (Nominated): Madam, India is a key player

of work. The Supreme Court of India, in a landmark Judgement in M. C. Mchta vs.

better India to accomplish this task. Constitutional mandate is provided in Articles 
23,24, 39(e), 41,45 (now 2 la) and the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation)  
Act of 1986. The Supreme Court directed the State to take immediate steps for 
eradication and rehabilitation of child labour, including imposition of sanctions

offenders, laid down by the Supreme Court six years ago, the problem of child labour 
would have been on its last legs by now. I urge upon the Government to ensure that the 
Supreme Court's directions are followed, in toto, in a time-bound frame.

SHRI  INDRAMONI BORA (Assam): Madam Deputy Chairperson, I beg to draw the 
attention of the hon. Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Law Minister to 
scrap the Illegal Migrants Determination by Tribunal Act of 1983. Madam, there has

in certain concentrated pockets in Assam.

help and patronage of a particular political party have become voters and have 
become a decisive factor in the political power in Assam.

was enacted known as Illegal Migrants Determination by Tribunal Act, 1983 
(Act XIII of 1983). This Act has an overriding effect over Passport Act of 1920 
and 1967, Foreigners Act, 1946, and the Immigrants (Expulsion from Assam) Act, 
1950. As per IMDT Act, an illegal migrant means a person who has entered in 
India on or after 25th March, 1971 and a foreigner has been defined in Foreigners 
Act. 1946 as one who has entered in India without any passport or any valid 
document.

the task has virtually become impossible. The onus of providing proof of a 
foreigner has to be given by the complainant himself. This act is discriminatory 
as it is only applicable to Assam. Due to procedures only 1485 persons could be 
deported in the course of last 20 years at the expenditure of Rs. 300 crores. This 
Act should immediately be scrapped by proper legislation to save Assam from 
infiltrators. Thank you, Madam for giving me this opportunity.

SHRI LAUTBHAI MEHTA (Gujarat): Madam, out of 358 Urban Co-operative Banks 
in Gujarat, 14 banks are under liquidation; in 18 banks, administrators have been

of confidence in the Urban Co-operative Banking Sector has led to premature 
withdrawals of deposits on the one side and poor recovery on the other side. The crisis 
has worsened the situation and, as a result, many banks are not in a position 'o 
maintain their liquidity. 
The Urban Co-operative Banks in Gujarat have deposits worth Rs. 15,000 crores 
and advances worth Rs. 11,000 crores. The banks, which are adversely affected due to 
various reasons have deposits worth Rs.2,500 crores. If these banks are liquidated, 
then, the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (DICGCI) has 
to pay ahuge sum of Rs.2,500 crores as a part of insurance coverage.

DICGCI should provide a soft loan of Rs. 1,000 crores, on the insured deposits of these 
banks, to enable these banks to maintain their liquidity and to strengthen their day-to-day 
operations. This will decrease the overall liability of DICGCI, restore public confidence 
and strengthen the urban banking sector in Gujarat which plays a pivotal role in trade, 
small, medium and self-employed sector financing and rendering social service at large.

Need to provide timely Medical Care to                                    
Victims of Road Accidents 
DR. DASARJ NARAYANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, as informed in 1998 
as many as 76,732 persons were killed in road accidents. This figure was 81,036 in 1999 
and 80,118 in 2000. Majority of accident victims could be saved if timely medical help is 
provided to them. But, unfortunately, when an accident occurs, no passer-by comes 
forward to help the helpless victim because"of fear of harassment by police later. Even if 
some good Samaritan takes the victim to a hospital, nursing home or clinic of a doctor, 
medical attention is not given, because it being a medico legal case. The victim is not 
attended unless the police arrives and registers a case. By the time medical treatment 
starts, it is too late and victim loses his life. 
Though Supreme Court recently has observed that accident victim should be given 
immediate medical treatment without waiting for registration of a medico •egal case and 
good Samaritans bringing victim to hospital etc. should not be harassed. But this 
direction of apex court has not percolated to hospitals, nursing homes, clinics etc. and 
more so to police personnel. 
Hence, I demand from the Government that:— 
Wide publicity be given to the Supreme Court judgement through 
Doordarshan, AIR and through advertisements in the print media and other 
TV channels be requested to give publicity on humanitarian aspects so that 
road accident victims get immediate medical attention and dieir saviours 
are not harassed by police; 
Trauma Centres be opened in all hospitals up to district levels; 
Ambulances with emergency medical equipments be stationed at 
conspicuous places; and 
Road discipline be strictly imposed to reduce accidents on roads and 
highways.

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: As the hon. Minister has explained that the 
recommendation of the Standing Committee is being accepted and it is technical. However, 
the importance of the Bill is there because it relates to children and feeding infants 
regulatroy. I have a number of names. I would suggest that if Members want to speak, 
they can give only suggestions, instead of making long preliminary speeches. All of us 
know its importance. Please, if you have any suggestions, kindly give. But, the 
speeches must be short. The time allotted for this Bill is half- an hour, but I can 
always extend it. 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA( Kamataka) : Madam, the recent 
developments and findings of international agencies as well as researchers have revealed 
that infant thrives best on exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life and 
continued breastfeeding, together with complementary foods, for the first two years. The 
child should be adequately nourished to attain and maintain his health and development. 
Breast milk is an ideal food for the babies because it contains all the nutrients that a baby 
needs for first six months of life. Mother's milk is quickly and easily digested and it 
contains fat, lactose protein, vitamins, minerals and water that are necessay for the growth of 
baby. So, the milk substitute can be used after six months of life, along with mother's milk for 
about one to two years. Malnutrition is a major contributory factor of high incidence of 
infant mortality and physical and mental handicaps. The anti-infective properties of 
mother's milk protect infants against diseases. Breastfeeding is a natural process. Many 
NGOs are working for the promotion of this. Mother's milk is a complete food for 
newborn babies up to six months. If the mother's milk is properly fed, the babies will be 
healthy and it develops immunity in them to fight diseases which sometimes cause 
infants' death. Now a days, we find that the bottled water is contaminated and unfit 
for consumption. Then, Madam, please think about the life of so many infants using milk 
prepared by companies by using this type of water. Most of the time, feeding bottle, which is 
used to feed milk, will be used to feed juice, soup etc.If the bottle is not washed properly 
one can imagine the problems that cause to baby's health. 
Breastfeeding is the best form of infant nutrition. Unfortunately, there has been a 
steady decline due to various reasons. The practice of breastfeeding, in addition to 
satisfying the nutritional needs of the baby, also creates a strong mother-child bonding. 
Not only the pressures of urban life creat stress on woman but also the distance between 
workplace and residence makes the mother unable to reach her baby during the day. The 
work forces mother to use milk substitutes. 
238 

[ 7 May, 2003 ] RAJYA SABHA 
The multinational companies manufacturing infant milk substitutes and infant 
foods are not only using media and other advertising methods to promote their products 
but these industries are even using health professionals like doctors and nurses to 
promote their products and advise mothers on bottle-feeding.. The doctors, nurses 
and hospitals have more influence on pregnant women, nursing mother and their 
families than other members. In the absence of a strong interventions designed to protect, 
promote and support breastfeeding, the millions of infants are a greater risk of 
malnutrition, infections and deaths. Thus, there is a need to raise public awareness 
about the importance of breastfeeding as a right to both mother and child. 
It is significant to note that the World Health Organisation (WHO) and United 
Nations International Children's Fund (UNICEF) have played a catalytic role in the 
campaign through advocacy, information and social mobilization. The Government, 
health professionals and voluntary organizations should join in influencing individual 
families and communities in favour of breastfeeding. I am supporting this Bill saying 
that the milk substitute and milk food can be used only after the baby is six 
months old. Thank You.

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: We should also understand the ambit of the Bill. 
What is this Bill about? There is no dispute that breast-feeding is better than other 
milk substitutes. There is no dispute about it now. The Hon. Minister has also just now 
mentioned that. So, try to talk on the subject itself. Shrimati N.P. Durga. 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, it is estimated that 156.4 
million children are malnourished all over the world, and 10 per cent of them are found in the 
Asia-Pacific Region. And among these Asia-Pacific countries, India has the highest 
number of children who are malnourished. And this Bill, I am sure, will reduce 
malnourishment, encourage continued breast-feeding, and prohibit all forms of 
advertisements and promotion of infant milk substitutes and infant foods in the market. 
Infant malnutrition is a major contributory cause of high incidence of infant mortality, 
morbidity, and physical and mental handicaps. As per the scientific reasoning, mother 
and infant form a "biological unit,' and the breast-feeding is an integral part of 
reproductive process. This is a natural and ideal way of feeding the infant, and it 
provides a unique biological and emotional basis for a healthy development of a child. 
The antibodies in the milk of mother protect the infant against diseases. So, we have to 
educate the people by clearly explaining them the health hazards involved in feeding 
with bottles and using milk substitutes. There is also a need to bring awareness 
about breast-feeding as a right both for mother and child. I particularly welcome the 
amendments proposed to Section 2 and 3 of the parent Act. But. I fail to understand 
why the Hon. Minister wants to increase the age under Clause 2(iii)(f) from four 
months to six months. I think, this four months period is appropriate. Anyway, I shall be 
highly obliged if he could explain the reasons behind this increase, apart from the 
WHO Resolution. 
The next point is that a majority of the baby food manufacturing companies in India 
are multinationals, and they are based in other countries. So, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister as to how he is going to control those companies and how he is going to put 
restrictions on advertising baby food on the international channels, such as, BBC, 
CNN, CNBC, etc., which are beamed into the country under Clause 2(a) of the Bill. I 
would also like to know how the Hon. Minister is going to contain the international 
chain of agencies which are very well aware of the psyche of India. You can very 
well contain the Indian

it is just the technical details wliich arc being added to the Bill that has already been 
discussed. In all fairness, we should have really passed it without any discussion. But, I

oppose what the Minister suggests, and the very few instances, at least in my case, 
when we totally agree with what he is

saying, I think, we should give him all our support. So, I rise to support the 
Bill. 
Madam, in spite of the Government's continued efforts, the infant mor-
tality rate continues to be very high in India. It is estimated that India has the 
highest number of malnourished children in the world, and two-thirds of the 
babies bom have low birth weight because health is inno party's political agenda, 
and women's health even less so. It is seen that the number of mothers who die 
due to pregnancy-related issues alone in one week in India is more than that in 
all of Europe in a whole year. These are just related to pregnancy. Actually, 
experts have estimated that 70 per cent of these deaths are entirely preventable. 
What we are saying, in fact, is that the number of women we lose in one year in 
India is the same as having 300 airplane crashes a year. Can you imagine what 
would happen? Governments would fall if that were true. But Because it is a 
matter of women and their health,—it is, especially, the rural women who are 
dying—nobody is taking any notice. Now, as regards population stabilisation, 
as the hon. Members before me have said, when this is a matter of such concern 
to us, we have to see how infant mortality and maternal mortality are really 
connected with this issue. Even for population stabilisation, we have to ensure 
both, control on maternal mortality and infant mortality. 
The WHO has found—based on findings of international agencies 
and researchers—that ideally the infant thrives best on exclusive breast feeding 
for the first six months of life as well as continued breast feeding together with 
complementary food for the first two years. However, advertising campaigns, 
which promote infant milk substitutes, feeding bottles and infant foods, work on 
the psyche of the feeding mother, in such a way, as to promote a feeling of 
tremendous inadequacy in her. She is fooled into believing that milk substitutes 
will ensure better health for her child and she starts feeding her infant with this, 
in spite of, hardly being able to afford it. Moreover, it becomes worse because 
rural women do not have facilities to sterilise the feeding bottles and nipples, 
etc. All of us know how safe is drinking water in our country, particularly in rural 
areas. We have the dubious distinction of ranking amongst the lowest in quality 
of drinking water. Most mothers do not even use the three tablespoons, they 
use much less than the quantity that is required because of the poor awareness 
levels. Now, we are aware that diarrhoea remains a major cause of infant deaths 
and contributes to the high incidence,as faulty practice associated with misuse 
253 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003] 
of milk powder whi ch, advertising promotes. Now, I am not normally in favour of banning 
anything, because I feel that instead of banning something, we really should be able to 
produce counter-images, and then make people aware. But in this one instance, I think all 
liberal people would also make an exception and say just as we talk about banning 
advertising which promotes the use of tobacco, or promotes the use of alcohol, or 
promotes the use of drugs, in the same way, this would be one of those few instances 
where we would say that, 'Yes', banning is justified. But, however, it is extremely 
important to see that these counter-images that we create, promoting breastfeeding are 
done with a lot of sensitivity. It is wonderful that we herald motherhood; we say all the 
wonderful things that have been said here, but I think we have to do it very carefully. We 
must understand another tiling. In the advertising, there is a danger that you will fixate 
women only in her capacity as a mother and celebrate that. But what we are saying, it is 
wonderful to celebrate her as, a mother, but she is an entity in her own right and all her 
aspects should be celebrated. That is extremely important that we say that a woman is 
also more than just a mother and it is also important that the counter-images are done 
with sensitivity, so that in certain instances when mothers are not able to provide 
breastfeeding, simply because they have constraints of time, they have to be working 
mothers, they should not be made to feel guilty about it It is very easy to turn this into a 
black and white and say you are a wonderful mother, only if you breastfeed, and, if you do 
not do it, you feel guilty. So, it is extremley important that we create these counter-
images, recognising that a woman's right to be a mother is to be celebrated. But a woman is 
a woman in her entirety, and, in certain instances, either she is not able to produce 
enough milk to breastfeed the baby or there are other constraints on her, and it has to 
be done in way that the blame game is not apportioned to her. That is my only 
suggestion. Thank you, very much.

SHRIH. K. JAVARE GOWDA (Kamataka): Madam, I would like to 
welcome the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of 
Production, Supply and Distribution) Amendment Bill, 2003. After the introductory 
speech made by, the hon. Minister and the speeches made by learned colleagues, I am 
of the view that whatever suggestions that were given, are all acceptable. 
254 

[7 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Also, the intention of this Bill is very clear, and the intention is to 
promote the interests of the child, But the basic point is about the mothers. I 
would categorise mothers in our country into two categories, the middle-class 
mothers and the BPL mothers, those belonging to families living Below the 
Poverty Line. When we are talking about this Bill, we have to look at the condi-
tion of the BPL mothers. They do not have any food for feeding themselves. 
They do not get nutritious food. How can we provide nutritious food to 
mothers? Of course, this Ministry is not responsible for that. The entire society 
and the economic condition of the country are responsible for that. Anyway, 
whatever is the situation at present, this Bill has been introduced to improve the 
situation, and regulate the production, supply and distribution of infant milk 
substitutes, feeding bottles and infant foods. So. I welcome this Bill. 
Madam, I want to suggest one thing. Many of the women Members 
who spoke before me may not agree with me. But I want to sincerely suggest that 
we should educate the educated mothers. Why? Look at the women living in the 
urban areas, and the women belonging to economically upper-class families in 
the villages; they do not want to breastfeed their children. If, at all, they do feed 
their children, they do it only for a couple of months, because they have the 
impression that they will lose their health, or, their beauty— I am afraid to say it, 
but I have no option either. Every woman brings up her child in this way. But for 
that we have to contain these substitutes being sold by multinationals. This is 
very important. Look at the advertisements; how beautiful ads they give, claim-
ing that their products, or milk substitutes provide more nutrition than a mother's 
milk! I would like to tell'you one thing. That is about the immunisation capabili-
ties of a mother's milk. My mother is uneducated. She is a villager. I drank my 
mother's milk for three years or more. I got immunised in the real way, when I 
was a kid. Nowadays. I don't think any mother breastfeeds her child for more 
than a year, or even six months. Madam, a movement is required in the society. 
Merely by passing such a Bill, I don't think we will be able to remove this type of 
a misconception. Therefore, it is a good piece of legislation. I request the 
Ministry that a special branch should be opened in the Ministry to launch 
awareness campaigns for mothers to educate them that it is their 
responsibility to breastfeed their children. Also, it is the responsibility of the 
society to see to it that the BPL mothers are provided with the required 
nutritious food.

maternity leave period should be increased. I am not supporting that. An alternative 
should be made available so as to enable the working mothers to feed their children, 
at least, up to six months. 
With these words, I welcome this Bill.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS AND

GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRIHARTN PATHAK): Madam Chairperson, I move: 
That the Bill further to amend the Foreigners Act, 1946, be taken into

The Foreigners (Amendment) Bill, 1998 was initially introduced in June 1998 
for amendment of Section 14 to enhance the punishment of imprisonment 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2003 ] 
for a maximum period from 5 years to 8 years. The Bill was referred to the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee of Ministry of Home 
Affairs for examination and report. The Committee deliberated and submitted 
its Report in March 2000. The Committee had favoured the holistic approach in 
dealing with the issue relating to illegal migration, especially with a view to 
undertake the comprehensive legislation to effectively deal with the problems 
of infiltration. Subsequently, the Ministry of Home Affairs referred the matter to 
the Law Comnussion of India for study and recommendations. Madam, the Law 
Commission of India presented its 175th Report on Foreigners (Amendment) 
Bill, 2000 to the Government in September 2000. The recommendations of the 
Law Commission were examined and the Government decided to pursue the 
Foreigners (Amendment) Bill, 1988 already introduced in the Rajya Sabha for 
enhancing existing maximum punishment from 5 years to 8 years which has also 
been recommended by the Law Commission. Contravention of the provision of 
the Foreigners Act, 1946 or of any order made thereunder or of any direction 
given in pursuance of that Act or such order is punishable with imprisonment, 
which may extend to five years and fine. The offences under the Foreigners Act 
are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by the First-Class Magistrate. Madam, 
however, these accused persons arrested under the said Act very often managed 
lo obtain bail under Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Further, the 
Act also does not clarify the violation of the various provisions of the Act or 
such order and only provides for punishment which may extend to five years 
and fine. The quantum of punishment for various offences is left to the discretion 
of the court. It is proposed to classify offences under the Foreigners Act and to 
provide for punishment depending on the gravity of offence committed. It is 
also proposed that the maximum punishment under the Foreigners Act may be 
up to 8 years and fine be raised from Rs. 10.000 to Rs. 50,000. The enhancement 
of the punishment will have the following effects. Firstly, serious offences will 
'become triable by the Court of Session. Formerly, it was triable by the First-
Class Magistrate. It was mentioned that, Madam, under Section 437 of the Code 
of Criminal Procedure accused persons^manage to get the bail. Secondly, (he 
Court will require giving notice to the State Government thereby affording it an 
opportunity to oppose the bail application under the provision of subsection 
(1) of Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. These are the two 
amendments. With these amendments, we have brought forward this Bill. In 
view of this, I commend this august House that the Bill may be taken up for 
consideration.

SHRIMATTLAL SARKAR (Tripura): Madam, the Amendment proposed is 
appreciable. The amendments are aimed at preventing unauthorised persons coming 
from the neighbouring countries. The amendment is aimed at preventing them from 
staying and settling beyond the legal period, whenever they come with permission.

who have illegally intruded into our country. Penalties have also been provided for those 
illegal immigrants. But the rule alone is not enough for banning infiltration and 
immigration. There may be various kinds of intruders into the country. Some people 
come here to take out their livelihood when there is economic crisis in any of our 
neighbouring countries. Poor labourers come into our country and this is treated or 
may be called the 'illegal import of manpower1. They come; they work here; they get 
wages, and thereby the wages of our own labourers are being lowered down. This is 
also one problem. They may not be coming for doing harm to our country, but even then, 
indirectly, harm is done. There are other types of persons coming through illegal 
means. They are miscreants, dacoits and other anti-social elements, who

SHRI FALI S. N ARIMAN (NOMINATED): Sir, I have no quarrel with 
the Bill. But, listening to the large number of hon. Members here, I think we all 
have some problem with how it is titled. I thought that we should have 
scrapped a British India Act, 1946, and introduced a comprehensive legislation 
with regard to people of foreign origin, that is, people who are not nationals 
of India. Particularly, in the context of the dual nationality, which is now 
proposed to be introduced in this country, there should be a more 
comprehensive legislation. I have no problem with dealing with criminals. But 
as one of my hon. colleagues said, and I think he is right, when you say you 
are amending the Foreigners' Act, in British India, everyone except the 
Britisher was a 'foreigner' - that is a pejorative term. And I would rather call 
this a Foreigners' Offences Act, so that you are dealing with offences, you are 
not dealing with foreigners. There are very fine foreigners who stay in India 
and who commit no offence. The most eminent foreigner was Mother Teresa, 
there was nothing wrong with her, she was one of our great gems. So, let us 
not give that impression, and this is what exactly we should not convey, that 
we are making life more difficult, more harassing for people who are of 
different nationalities, who live in India, who carry on work in India, and as 
my friend said, who invest capital in India, and against whom there is no 
offence or charge, and who are particularly welcome in India. In fact, in our 
Constitution, article 14, article 21 and article 25, they all guarantee fundamental 
rights to persons; not only to citizens. The right to equality, the right to be 
treated fairly, decently, that life and liberty should be protected, is not a 
guarantee to citizens only, but to all persons. Therefore, let us not forget the 
constitutional aspect on which we are here today, and the global image that 
we are projecting. And, therefore, I would recommend very strongly to the 
Minister that if he is making certain criminal provisions, penal provisions 
more stringent, introducing a larger punishment, I am all for it. But, let us not 
give the impression that this is foreigners. This is for foreigners' illegal acts; 
illegalities of foreigners. It has nothing to do with people who are decent and 
who are really welcome in this country. Therefore, Sir, I would also
